title: 9 Things EVERY Christmas Guest Room Needs (Your Guests NOTICE)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, I've hosted family for Christmas for over fifty years. Sons, daughters-in-law, grandchildren, my brother Danny and his snoring, and one year a cousin from Iowa I'd never met who stayed nine days. And I've learned that people don't remember how fancy your house was. They remember how you made them feel when they woke up in it.
scenes.caption: HOW YOU MADE THEM FEEL

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you nine things every Christmas guest room needs, and they cost almost nothing. Little things your guests will notice, and remember, and tell everybody about. And stay with me, because the last one is the thing my Aunt Margaret did for every guest, and people still talk about it sixty years later.
scenes.caption: NINE THINGS

scenes.text: My Aunt Margaret lived in Columbus, in a big old house with a spare room at the top of the stairs. When we visited at Christmas, I got to sleep there, all by myself, in a bed with a white chenille spread and a hot water bottle tucked under the covers. I was nine years old, and I felt like a princess in a hotel.
scenes.caption: LIKE A PRINCESS

scenes.text: She didn't have money, honey. Uncle Walt drove a bread truck. But she thought about everything a guest might need in the middle of the night, and she put it right there before you had to ask. That's the whole secret of a good guest room. In a minute I'll show you the first thing, and it's the one most hosts forget.
scenes.caption: BEFORE YOU HAVE TO ASK

scenes.text: And here's the best way to find out what your guest room needs. Sleep in it yourself, one night, before the company comes. You'll find out the mattress sags, the lamp is too far from the bed, the closet has no hangers, and the window lets in a draft. I did this in nineteen seventy-five, and I fixed eleven things the next morning.
scenes.caption: SLEEP IN IT YOURSELF

scenes.text: Number one, the one most hosts forget. A lamp right by the bed, that you can turn on without getting up. And a little nightlight in the hallway, and one in the bathroom. A guest in a strange house at three in the morning, looking for the bathroom in the dark, is how people stub toes and walk into closets. My cousin from Iowa walked into my linen closet and stood there for a full minute.
scenes.caption: A LIGHT BY THE BED

scenes.text: Number two. Extra blankets, folded at the foot of the bed, or in a basket where they can see them. Everybody sleeps different. Some people are always cold, and they're too polite to ask for another blanket. So they lie there shivering all night. A soft throw and a heavy quilt, right there, means nobody has to ask. And an extra pillow, a soft one and a firm one.
scenes.caption: NOBODY HAS TO ASK

scenes.text: Number three. A stack of fresh towels on the bed or a chair, so they know which ones are theirs. A bath towel, a hand towel and a washcloth for each person. And a little basket with the things people forget. A new toothbrush, small toothpaste, soap, shampoo, a razor, a comb, aspirin, and a phone charger. I keep the little soaps from hotels all year for this basket.
scenes.caption: THE THINGS PEOPLE FORGET

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. And put a phone charger by the bed, with a long cord. It's the first thing every guest under sixty asks for today. My grandson says a guest room without a charger is like a guest room without a bed. I think he's exaggerating, but only a little.
scenes.caption: A CHARGER BY THE BED

scenes.text: Number four. Room to put their things. Clear out half the closet, and leave a few empty hangers. Empty one drawer in the dresser. Put a luggage rack, or just a sturdy chair or a bench, where they can open their suitcase without bending to the floor. Living out of a suitcase on the floor for a week is the worst part of visiting anybody.
scenes.caption: EMPTY HANGERS

scenes.text: And a mirror, honey, a full-length one if you can, on the back of the door. And a small table or a cleared spot on the dresser where they can set out their things, their glasses, their watch, their pills. Older guests especially. My mother, when she visited me in her eighties, needed a place for her pills, her glasses and her Bible, all in a row. So I cleared the dresser top every Christmas, just for her.
scenes.caption: A PLACE FOR THEIR THINGS

scenes.text: Number five. A glass and a pitcher or bottle of water on the nightstand. And a little plate of Christmas cookies or a small bowl of candy with a napkin. People get thirsty and a little hungry in the night, and they don't want to go wandering through your kitchen in their nightgown. Aunt Margaret left two of her sugar cookies on a doily, every single night.
scenes.caption: TWO SUGAR COOKIES

scenes.text: Number six. A little bit of Christmas in the room. Not much. A small wreath on the door, a sprig of greenery in a jar, a tiny lit tree on the dresser, or a candle. Just enough so it feels like part of the celebration, not a storage room with a bed in it. My guest room gets one little ceramic Christmas tree with colored lights, from nineteen seventy. The grandchildren fight to sleep next to it.
scenes.caption: A LITTLE CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: So far, a light by the bed, extra blankets, towels and a basket, room in the closet, water and a snack, and a little Christmas. Number seven. A little card with the information they need. The Wi-Fi password. What time breakfast is. Which bathroom is theirs. Where the coffee is, if they get up early. It saves them from asking a dozen awkward questions.
scenes.caption: THE WI-FI PASSWORD

scenes.text: And tell them about the early riser, honey. In my house, it's me. I'm up at five-thirty. So I put a note on the card that says, Grandma is up early, the coffee is on by six, come down any time, and don't you dare make your bed. That last line always makes them smile. And they make the bed anyway.
scenes.caption: DON'T MAKE YOUR BED

scenes.text: Number eight. Quiet and privacy. A door that closes and stays closed. Dark curtains, or an extra blanket you can hang over the window, so they can sleep past dawn. And a little fan or a sound machine to cover the sounds of a busy house. Especially if Uncle Danny is snoring down the hall. Danny's snoring has been measured. It's louder than a lawnmower.
scenes.caption: LOUDER THAN A LAWNMOWER

scenes.text: And give them time alone, sweetheart. When family comes for several days, everybody needs a little rest from everybody else. Don't plan every hour. Let them sleep late, take a walk, read in their room, or take a nap after lunch. A good host knows when to leave her guests alone. My mother said, company is like fish. After three days, give them some air.
scenes.query: woman reading in guest room chair
scenes.caption: GIVE THEM SOME AIR

scenes.text: And now number nine, Aunt Margaret's secret, the one people still talk about. A handwritten note on the pillow. Just a few lines. Welcome home, we're so glad you're here. Sleep well. And one little personal thing. I remember the first Christmas you came here. Or, I made your favorite pie for tomorrow. That's all. It takes two minutes to write.
scenes.caption: A NOTE ON THE PILLOW

scenes.text: When I was nine, Aunt Margaret's note on my pillow said, Ruthie, you are my favorite niece, but don't tell your cousins. I believed it for thirty years. Then at her funeral, in nineteen eighty-six, all eleven of us cousins found out she'd written the exact same note to every single one of us. We laughed and cried all afternoon. She was right. We were all her favorite.
scenes.caption: WE WERE ALL HER FAVORITE

scenes.text: And on the last morning, a little something for the road. A small tin of cookies, a few sandwiches wrapped in wax paper, or a thermos of coffee for a long drive. Aunt Margaret always sent us home with a shoebox of fried chicken and a pound cake. We ate it in the car before we got out of Columbus. My father said it was the best part of the whole trip.
scenes.caption: SOMETHING FOR THE ROAD

scenes.text: And if you don't have a guest room, honey, you can still do all of this. Make up the sofa bed or an air mattress in the den, with real sheets, a good pillow and a quilt. Put a little lamp beside it, a basket with towels, water and a note. Hang a sheet on a tension rod for privacy. A well-made sofa bed with a note is better than a fancy room nobody thought about.
scenes.query: made up sofa bed quilt lamp
scenes.caption: THE SOFA BED

scenes.text: And make it easy on yourself, sweetheart. Wash the sheets and towels the week before, and get the room ready two days early, so you're not making beds at midnight on Christmas Eve when the car pulls in. Then shut the door and don't touch it. Your guests will walk in and think you did it all by magic.
scenes.caption: BY MAGIC

scenes.text: So one more time. Sleep in it yourself first. A lamp by the bed and nightlights in the hall. Extra blankets and pillows. Towels, and a basket of forgotten things, with a charger. Room in the closet. Water and two cookies. A little Christmas. A card with the Wi-Fi and the coffee. Quiet and dark curtains. And a handwritten note on the pillow. That's how Aunt Margaret made every one of us feel like her favorite.
scenes.caption: EVERYBODY'S FAVORITE

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Who's coming to your house for Christmas this year? Or are you the one traveling? The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WHO'S COMING THIS YEAR?
